title: Trump-Thune Clash Escalates as White House Warns Patience 'Running Out' on Election Bill
excerpt: The public spat between the president and the Senate majority leader over the stalled SAVE America Act exposes deepening Republican fractures ahead of the 2026 midterms.
body:
• White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said Trump's patience with Senate Majority Leader John Thune is "running out" over the stalled SAVE America Act.
  • Thune fired back, telling the White House to "get on the phone and get the votes" instead of blaming Senate Republicans.
  • The bill faces a math problem: all Senate Democrats oppose it, and at least four Republicans have voted against it.

White House Takes Aim at Thune

The simmering tension between President Donald Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune erupted into a public confrontation on July 23, with the White House declaring that the president's patience with the South Dakota Republican is "running out" over his inability to pass the SAVE America Act.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=pShJpE3fA94

"His patience is running out. He wants to see as much of the SAVE America Act passed as possible by the August recess," White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters. "The House did its job. The Senate needs to do its job, too."

The remarks followed Trump singling out Thune by name at a rally in Marietta, Georgia, on July 22, where the president urged the crowd to call the senator directly and demanded the Senate "terminate the filibuster."

"Everybody call John Thune at the Senate — he's the leader of the Republican Party — and tell him to get this stuff approved."

— Donald Trump, at a rally in Marietta, Georgia

Trump also called the Senate "a place that you send things when you want them to die."

Thune Pushes Back

Thune wasted little time responding. Speaking to reporters at the Capitol on Thursday, the majority leader directed his frustration at the White House.

"She or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right? So instead of pointing the finger at Republicans, they might think about going after the people who are stopping it on the floor, which is the Democrats."

— John Thune, Senate Majority Leader

When asked what the White House's motivation might be for publicly blaming him, Thune offered a blunt reply: "I wish I had a good answer for that."

Senate Republicans rallied behind their leader. Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina said he had "1,000% confidence in Thune" and that "anybody in the White House who thinks he's not a good leader isn't qualified for their job," according to USA Today.

The Math Problem

The SAVE America Act — which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote, mandate photo ID at the polls, and restrict universal mail-in voting — has passed the House three times but repeatedly stalled in the Senate.

The core obstacle is arithmetic. The Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold requires Democratic support, but every Senate Democrat opposes the legislation. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, far short of the 60 needed.

Trump has pushed to eliminate the filibuster entirely, but at least four Senate Republicans — Susan Collins of Maine, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and Tillis — voted against adding the legislation to a Republican budget package in June. Even under a simple-majority vote, the bill may lack 50 votes.

House Tries a New Route

House Speaker Mike Johnson attempted to break the logjam on July 22, pushing through a $95 billion budget reconciliation package on a razor-thin 216-214 vote. The framework includes $10 billion to incentivize states to implement elements of the SAVE Act, according to Politico.

Reconciliation bypasses the filibuster, requiring only a simple majority. But the Senate parliamentarian could rule that voting overhaul provisions do not meet the strict budgetary requirements of the process.

Thune has been openly skeptical. When Johnson suggested Congress could deliver the bill before the August recess, Thune told reporters on July 16 that it was "news to him," adding: "I have to be the realist. I can't make any guarantees over here."

What's Next

The clash is unfolding less than four months before the November midterms, with Republicans at risk of losing their narrow congressional majorities. Tillis challenged the urgency, saying some Republicans were "being dishonest to the American people to say that we need SAVE Act passed because there's no way on God's green Earth it can be implemented by the election," according to Fox News.

The $95 billion reconciliation package now moves to the Senate, where its fate is uncertain. With the August recess approaching and Trump's public pressure intensifying, the standoff is likely to escalate further — testing Republican unity heading into a consequential election season.
